quote: Residual negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition, alogia) have persisted on both trials.
problem: The only residual symptoms named are negative symptoms, yet the item keys clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Treatment resistance and clozapine's evidence base rest on persistent positive symptoms; clozapine has no established advantage for primary negative symptoms, and add-on antidepressants (distractor B) have modest meta-analytic support for negative symptoms. The stem also omits confirmed adherence, which TRRIP requires to exclude pseudo-resistance.
whyItMatters: Learners infer that residual negative symptoms alone after two trials mandate clozapine, and the antidepressant distractor becomes defensible, so the key is no longer clearly the only best answer.
evidence: Howes et al., TRRIP consensus, Am J Psychiatry 2017 (two adequate trials, confirmed adherence, specify symptom domain); APA Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia 2020, clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; Helfer et al., Am J Psychiatry 2016 (antidepressant add-on for negative symptoms, small benefit).
correction: Persistent auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions, along with negative symptoms, have persisted on both trials despite confirmed adherence.

quote: The conclusion of CATIE: effectiveness is broadly comparable across FGAs and SGAs; the clinically actionable difference is in the side-effect profile matched to the patient's individual vulnerability.
problem: The stem concerns a first-episode patient, but CATIE enrolled people with chronic schizophrenia. The item applies CATIE to first-episode psychosis without saying so. Distractor D's opening clause ('CATIE only applies to chronic schizophrenia') is actually true, and the rationale never says which evidence covers first-episode patients.
whyItMatters: Learners come away believing CATIE studied first-episode patients, and a careful examinee may be penalised for noticing the population mismatch.
evidence: Lieberman et al., NEJM 2005 (CATIE; chronic schizophrenia); Kahn et al., Lancet 2008 (EUFEST, first-episode: symptom reduction comparable across agents, with lower discontinuation on SGAs than on low-dose haloperidol).
correction: The conclusion of CATIE (chronic schizophrenia; first-episode trials such as EUFEST point the same way): effectiveness is broadly comparable across FGAs and SGAs; the clinically actionable difference is in the side-effect profile matched to the patient's individual vulnerability.

quote: In a young adult with new-onset psychosis, the organic yield is highest at the first episode.
problem: The stem has a team 'ready to diagnose schizophrenia' after 3 weeks of symptoms, and the rationale never corrects this. DSM-5-TR schizophrenia requires 6 months of continuous signs. At 3 weeks the working primary diagnosis would be brief psychotic disorder, or schizophreniform disorder if it lasts longer.
whyItMatters: Learners may believe schizophrenia can be diagnosed once secondary causes are excluded, whatever the duration.
evidence: DSM-5-TR Schizophrenia Criterion C (≥6 months); Brief psychotic disorder (≥1 day, <1 month); Schizophreniform disorder (1–6 months).
correction: In a young adult with new-onset psychosis, the organic yield is highest at the first episode. Note also that 3 weeks of symptoms cannot meet the DSM-5-TR 6-month duration criterion for schizophrenia.

quote: without any major mood episode (depressive, manic, or mixed)
problem: DSM-5/DSM-5-TR removed the 'mixed episode'. Schizoaffective Criterion B specifies the absence of a major mood episode (depressive or manic). Mixed features is now a specifier, not an episode type. The same rationale also cites 'DSM-5' rather than DSM-5-TR.
whyItMatters: This reinforces DSM-IV terminology that no longer exists in the current manual.
evidence: DSM-5-TR Schizoaffective Disorder Criterion B; 'with mixed features' specifier.
correction: without any major mood episode (depressive or manic)

quote: One partially-dosed trial does not qualify.
problem: The stem's trial was risperidone 4 mg/day for 6 weeks, which is within the usual therapeutic range. The trial fails the threshold because it is a single trial, not because it was underdosed. Calling it 'partially-dosed' teaches that 4 mg/day risperidone is subtherapeutic.
whyItMatters: Learners may escalate risperidone above a standard effective dose on the belief that 4 mg is inadequate.
evidence: APA Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia 2020 (risperidone usual dose range); Leucht et al., Am J Psychiatry 2020 dose-response meta-analysis.
correction: A single trial, even at an adequate dose, does not qualify.

quote: Agitation = antipsychotic, Fever = infection, and Treat and wait all delay the single most important intervention: stopping the antipsychotic.
problem: Distractor D (benzodiazepine, then recheck) is wrong because it leaves the antipsychotic running and delays escalation. The rationale does not say that benzodiazepines (lorazepam) are an appropriate part of NMS supportive care once the antipsychotic has been stopped.
whyItMatters: Learners may conclude that benzodiazepines are contraindicated in NMS and withhold a first-line supportive treatment.
evidence: Strawn, Keck & Caroff, Am J Psychiatry 2007 (NMS management: stop the agent, supportive care, lorazepam; dantrolene/bromocriptine for severe cases).
correction: Agitation = antipsychotic, Fever = infection, and Treat and wait all delay the single most important intervention: stopping the antipsychotic (a benzodiazepine is reasonable supportive care in NMS, but only alongside stopping the antipsychotic and escalating care).

quote: A chain analysis — walking the sequence of antecedents, emotions, and behaviors with the patient non-punitively — turns the incident into a clinical formulation and a coping plan; this is the DBT standard and replaces documentation-only or punitive responses.
problem: The keyed response goes straight to chain analysis after self-harm on the unit. It omits wound assessment and treatment and a brief reassessment of suicidal intent and lethality (including securing the implement), which come first. Rejecting distractor C also implies that raising observation after self-harm is itself wrong, when a clinically indicated observation change is legitimate and only the punitive privilege restriction is not.
whyItMatters: Learners may start a chain analysis before the wound has been assessed or before checking whether the act carried suicidal intent that changes the level of observation.
evidence: Linehan DBT manual (chain analysis in the next session, after matter-of-fact medical care); NICE NG225 Self-harm 2022 (medical assessment and psychosocial assessment after self-harm).
correction: After wound care and a brief reassessment of suicidal intent, a chain analysis — walking the sequence of antecedents, emotions, and behaviors with the patient non-punitively — turns the incident into a clinical formulation and a coping plan; this is the DBT standard and replaces documentation-only or punitive responses.

quote: Without the patient's consent, do not confirm or share specific diagnosis or medication information.
problem: This states a stricter rule than federal law. HIPAA 45 CFR 164.510(b) allows disclosure to a family member involved in care if the patient, given the opportunity, does not object, and allows it on professional judgment when the patient is incapacitated or it is an emergency. Many states add stricter mental-health confidentiality statutes, and 42 CFR Part 2 is stricter for SUD records. The best practical step, asking the patient whether she agrees, is not mentioned.
whyItMatters: Learners may withhold information from families of incapacitated patients when HIPAA permits sharing, or may not think to ask the patient for permission. Neither the federal floor nor the state variation is taught.
evidence: 45 CFR 164.510(b)(1)–(3); HHS OCR guidance 'HIPAA Privacy Rule and Sharing Information Related to Mental Health' (2017).
correction: Without the patient's agreement, do not confirm or share specific diagnosis or medication information; ask the patient whether she agrees to sharing (HIPAA permits disclosure to involved family if she does not object, or on clinical judgment if she lacks capacity, but state law may be stricter).

quote: Psychoeducation — the hardest inpatient numbers for readmission prevention: readmission NNT 5 (Xia, Cochrane 2011) and relapse NNT 9; and it costs nothing except time.
problem: The NNT 5 for readmission in Xia 2011 comes from only n=206 participants, in a review whose authors rate the trials as of limited quality and say the true effect is likely smaller. Calling it the 'hardest' (strongest) numbers, and in the pearl 'highest-evidence', misstates how certain the estimate is.
whyItMatters: Learners and QI teams are taught to treat a small, low-certainty subgroup estimate as the strongest evidence in inpatient psychiatry.
evidence: Xia J, Merinder LB, Belgamwar MR. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;CD002831 (doi:10.1002/14651858.CD002831.pub2): readmission n=206, RR 0.71, NNT 5 (CI 4–13); relapse n=1214, NNT 9; 'true size of effect is likely to be less'.
correction: Psychoeducation — the most directly readmission-relevant evidence: readmission NNT 5 (Xia, Cochrane 2011; small subset, n=206, limited-quality trials) and relapse NNT 9; and it costs nothing except time.

quote: The main barrier to family psychoeducation being delivered is clinician avoidance — structured family work is available to the minority of families who receive it largely because of clinician behavior, not family behavior.
problem: Eassom 2014, the source cited, locates the barriers in organisational culture, leadership, staff training and supervision, and staff reservations, not mainly in individual clinicians avoiding the work. 'Clinician avoidance' as the main barrier overstates and individualises a service-level finding.
whyItMatters: Learners and QI teams may treat low family-work rates as a matter of individual clinician attitude and miss the organisational fixes (leadership, workflow, training) the literature identifies.
evidence: Eassom E et al., BMJ Open 2014;4:e006108 (doi:10.1136/bmjopen-2014-006108): 'Organisational cultures and paradigms can work to limit family involvement… supported by strong leadership'; training necessary but not sufficient.
correction: The main barriers to family psychoeducation being delivered sit with clinicians and services — staff reservations, training gaps, and organisational culture — not with family refusal.

quote: Black patients face roughly 1.85× the adjusted odds of a restraint event on inpatient psychiatric units — this disparity is a quality-of-care issue, not an acuity artifact.
problem: Singal et al. is a single-system retrospective chart review (adolescents and adults), and its adjusted odds ratio cannot rule out residual confounding by acuity. The key asserts a causal conclusion ('not an acuity artifact') that the study does not establish. It also presents one health system's AOR as the general inpatient figure.
whyItMatters: Learners take away an overstated causal claim, which weakens their credibility when a colleague raises confounding. The accurate message (disparity persists after adjustment and warrants review) is strong enough on its own.
evidence: Singal S et al., Psychiatr Serv 2024;75(4):308-315 (doi:10.1176/appi.ps.20230057): retrospective review, n=29,739, one Northwell system; Black AOR 1.85.
correction: Black patients faced roughly 1.85× the adjusted odds of a restraint event in a large inpatient psychiatric sample — a disparity that persists after adjustment and should be treated as a quality-of-care issue.

quote: suicide risk peaks in the first week post-discharge (Chung et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2017)
problem: Chung et al. 2017 reports that the suicide rate is highest within the first 3 months after discharge. It does not analyse a first-week peak; that comes from a separate Chung et al. BMJ Open 2019 meta-analysis.
whyItMatters: The citation does not support the specific claim attributed to it.
evidence: Chung DT et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2017;74(7):694-702 (doi:10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2017.1044): 'highest within 3 months after discharge (1132 per 100,000 person-years)'.
correction: suicide risk is highest in the first 3 months post-discharge (Chung et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2017)

quote: Strong safety documentation names chronic factors, acute drivers, protective factors with limits, modifiable targets, and the current plan.
problem: The keyed 'strong' note contains no protective factors, so the model answer does not meet the rationale's own standard.
whyItMatters: Learners copying the keyed note as a template will leave out protective factors and their limits.
evidence: Internal consistency with pg_suicide.md documentation standard.
correction: Strong safety documentation names chronic factors, acute drivers, protective factors with limits (omitted in the keyed example for brevity — add them), modifiable targets, and the current plan.

quote: healthcare workers have lower rates of completed suicide than the general population.
problem: 'Completed suicide' is discouraged terminology; current usage is 'suicide death' or 'died by suicide'. Separately, nurses (especially female nurses) have higher suicide rates than the general population, so noting that would strengthen this stem about an ICU nurse.
whyItMatters: It models outdated language, and the rationale misses a relevant risk point about the stem patient's occupation.
evidence: Davis MA et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2021 (nurse suicide rates higher than the general population); AFSP/Reporting on Suicide language guidance.
correction: healthcare workers have lower suicide death rates than the general population.

quote: is the most evidence-based single intervention to reduce suicide death.
problem: The strongest evidence for reducing suicide deaths is for population-level restriction of means. The keyed option is individual lethal-means counselling, whose evidence is mainly for changes in storage behaviour, not suicide death. The rationale merges the two.
whyItMatters: The recommended action is correct, but learners may overstate the evidence base when they counsel or teach.
evidence: Zalsman G et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2016 (means restriction, population level); Mann JJ et al., JAMA 2005.
correction: is the single intervention with the strongest evidence for reducing suicide death (strongest at the population level; individual counseling mainly changes storage behavior).

quote: admitted for a first manic episode. His mother interrupts repeatedly: 'He does this every time he stops his medication
problem: The stem describes a first manic episode but has the mother describe a recurring pattern whenever he stops his medication. The two are internally inconsistent.
whyItMatters: This creates avoidable confusion about the history. Distractor C (correcting her 'factual inaccuracy') then reads as potentially valid.
correction: admitted for a recurrent manic episode. His mother interrupts repeatedly: 'He does this every time he stops his medication
